summary: The American Procurement Improvement Act of 2026 updates and renames the federal program governing procurement from entities employing individuals who are blind or have significant disabilities (commonly known as the AbilityOne Program). The bill renames the governing committee as the Commission for the Employment of Individuals Who are Blind or Have Significant Disabilities, updates definitions and criteria for qualified nonprofit agencies, adds employee professional development requirements, establishes new public notice and reporting standards, and sets rules for pricing and contract management.

affected_groups.effect: They are affected through updated employment definitions, required professional development initiatives, wage parity with nondisabled peers, and protections against involuntary or constructive termination resulting from program labor-hour compliance criteria.
affected_groups.group: Blind individuals and individuals with significant disabilities

affected_groups.effect: They must meet new criteria regarding direct labor hour percentages, employee professional development offerings, wage standards, and compliance monitoring, while being subject to updated authorization and potential revocation procedures.

They must comply with new procurement list notice requirements, follow updated pricing and negotiation rules, adhere to annual public reporting mandates regarding program procurement percentages, and ensure intergovernmental support agreements do not circumvent program rules.

key_provisions: Renames the Committee for Purchase From People Who Are Blind or Severely Disabled to the Commission for the Employment of Individuals Who are Blind or Have Significant Disabilities and updates related terminology throughout Title 41 of the United States Code.

Requires qualified nonprofit agencies participating in the program to employ participating employees for at least 51 percent of direct labor hours, provide employee professional development, and pay wages consistent with nondisabled peers doing the same or similar work.

Grants the Commission authority to add products or services to the procurement list for limited time periods up to 5 years, particularly for new lines of business or pilot projects, and establishes advance notice periods for additions and removals.
Mandates that federal agencies publicly report annually on the percentage of total contract funds obligated for products and services procured from the program list.

Permits the Administrator of General Services to use a governmentwide contract vehicle up to $50,000,000 total contract value for a single contract cycle when two or more qualified nonprofit agencies perform the same service.

Clarifies that participating employees of a qualified nonprofit agency are considered employees under all applicable federal, state, and local labor and employment laws, regardless of rehabilitative service client status.
missing_information: The specific operational costs or budgetary appropriations required to implement the new commission rules, reporting structures, and professional development technical assistance initiatives are not mentioned.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The American Procurement Improvement Act of 2026 updates and renames the federal program governing procurement from entities employing individuals who are blind or have significant disabilities (commonly known as the AbilityOne Program). The bill renames the governing committee as the Commission for the Employment of Individuals Who are Blind or Have Significant Disabilities, updates definitions and criteria for qualified nonprofit agencies, adds employee professional development requirements, establishes new public notice and reporting standards, and sets rules for pricing and contract management.
summary_detail.significance: The legislation modernizes the statutory framework of a federal procurement program that has operated for over 50 years. By revising definitions, establishing training and professional development standards, implementing wage parity rules, and setting new reporting and contract monitoring mechanisms, the bill alters federal purchasing procedures and employment oversight for agencies, participating nonprofits, and workers with significant disabilities.
